events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Isha proposes Isha, Omar. As leader on Mission 1 with no private information, I'm proposing a balanced two-person team that includes myself as a Loyal Servant, so the mission starts with a trusted member and the group can judge Omar's conduct from the mission outcome.

The team of Isha and Omar is a reasonable starting point since Isha, as leader, is willing to be on the first mission themselves. That said, I want to hear Omar's reasoning for being comfortable with this proposal — and Isha, why did you specifically choose Omar over the other available players? On Mission 1 with no information yet, I'd like us to establish some baseline trust signals before we commit. I don't have a strong objection to this team, but I'd feel better understanding the logic behind it. Others, what's your read on this pairing?

Zara, fair question. I chose Omar because on Mission 1 I have no information that separates the other players, so any second member is essentially a guess. I included myself so the team has a Loyal Servant who knows my own intent, and Omar's conduct on this mission will give us a concrete outcome to judge. I'm not claiming Omar is trustworthy. I'm saying this is the least-informed choice available, and I'd support a revision if someone has a specific reason to prefer a different pairing. Arjun and Theo, if either of you has a concern about this team, please state it so we can weigh it before the vote.

I don't see a concrete reason to reject Isha and Omar on Mission 1. Isha has explained that with no private information the second slot is a low-information choice, and including herself gives the team a member who can speak to her own intent. Omar is on the team, so the mission result will give us useful conduct data either way. I would rather not manufacture suspicion before any mission outcome exists. At this stage I am prepared to vote yes unless someone presents a specific, evidence-based objection.

Theo, I appreciate the measured read, and I agree that manufacturing suspicion before any outcome is counterproductive. That said, I want to raise one structural point: on Mission 1 we get essentially zero information from a success — a success just tells us the team didn't fail, which confirms nothing about individual loyalty since even an Evil player can submit Success. So the real value of Mission 1 is not in the data it produces but in establishing who we're willing to trust with future, higher-stakes proposals. Given that, I'd prefer a second member other than Omar — not because I have a specific reason to distrust him, but because rotating who gets included across early missions gives us broader coverage if we ever need to compare behavior across multiple team compositions. Arjun, you've been quiet this whole discussion. Do you have any reaction to this team, and would you prefer to be in Omar's slot for Mission 1?

Zara, thanks — I'll answer directly since you asked.

My honest position: as a Loyal Servant I have no private information at all, so I cannot separate Omar from anyone else on the basis of role or allegiance. My information set is identical to his, which means swapping him out for me would not improve the team's information quality in any way. On the narrow question of whether Omar is a bad choice, I have no evidence that he is — I only know he was the least-informed pick available to Isha, and she has said so plainly.

That said, Zara's structural point has merit and I want to respond to it on its own terms rather than dismiss it. The observation that a Mission 1 success tells us very little about individual loyalty is correct: with no fail card, success is consistent with every single player on the team being a Loyal Servant submitting Success, and it is equally consistent with a hidden Evil player choosing Success. So the real product of Mission 1 is not data about anyone; it is the group's willingness to lock in a set of people before anyone has done anything observable. If we can cheaply rotate who we pair with Isha across the early missions, we gain more opportunities to compare behavior across different compositions later, which is where suspicion actually becomes possible.

On that basis, if Isha is open to it, I would volunteer to take the second slot in place of Omar for Mission 1. My reasoning is not that I have anything against Omar — I have nothing against him, and I want to be clear that this is not a signal of distrust. It is that a two-person team containing Isha and one uninformed Loyal Servant is a perfectly sound baseline, and since I gain and lose exactly the same information as Omar would, the exchange is costless. Whatever coverage we want to build, we can build equally well with me in that seat, and I would rather be evaluated on my own subsequent conduct than sit out and be judged by inference.

Theo, I agree with your read that manufacturing suspicion before any outcome is a poor use of this discussion, and I won't do that here. My position is that the current team is acceptable as proposed, and that the alternative of Isha plus me is also acceptable and slightly preferable on the coverage argument Zara raised. Either way, I have no evidence-based objection and I expect to vote yes.

Isha, if you want to keep Omar, I support it; if you want the rotation I described, I support that too. The decision is genuinely low-stakes and I do not want to hold up the vote over it.

I’m still comfortable with the proposed team of Isha and Omar. Arjun’s rotation argument is fair in principle, and I appreciate that he volunteered without casting suspicion on Omar, but I don’t think Mission 1 is the place to force a change for coverage alone. The information difference between Omar and Arjun in that second slot is effectively nil from my perspective, and the current proposal already has a clear rationale: Isha is on the team and has been transparent about the low-information nature of her choice. Switching now would mainly create churn rather than improve our read. I’d rather keep the proposal as-is, see the mission result, and use later missions to rotate and compare conduct. I have no evidence-based objection to Omar, and I have no evidence-based objection to Arjun either; this is simply a preference for stability on the first proposal. I intend to vote yes on Isha and Omar.

Theo, I want to address your stability argument directly. You said the information difference between Omar and Arjun in that second slot is effectively nil from your perspective, and I agree. But if the information difference is genuinely nil, then switching costs us nothing, and Arjun's coverage argument gives us a small but real benefit — broader behavioral data across early missions. Preferring stability when two options are informationally equivalent means we're choosing based on something other than information, and I'd rather we be explicit about what that is before committing.

Arjun, your volunteering without casting suspicion on Omar was well-reasoned, and the rotation logic holds: starting early gives us more compositions to compare later, which is where actual deduction becomes possible.

Isha, you're the leader and the decision is yours — are you planning to keep the team as proposed, or would you consider swapping in Arjun for the coverage benefit?

Zara, to answer directly: I am keeping Isha and Omar as proposed for now. Arjun's rotation argument is reasonable, and I am not dismissing it. Omar is not a concern for me, and I am not casting suspicion on him. My reason is that Mission 1 gives us little information either way, so stability is a fair tiebreaker. I will still consider a revision after discussion if someone raises a specific, evidence-based reason to prefer another pairing. Otherwise, I will vote yes and we can use later missions to compare compositions.

Since my name is on this team, I want to speak directly rather than let the discussion settle around me. Zara asked me earlier for my reasoning on being comfortable with this proposal, and the answer is simple: I had no basis to object to it. Isha was transparent that the second slot was a low-information choice, and I have nothing in my own read of the table that contradicts that. I'm comfortable serving on Mission 1, and I understand that the outcome will be used to evaluate my conduct — that is exactly as it should be.

On the rotation question: Arjun's offer was gracious and his reasoning sound, and I want to be clear that I take it as no slight. But Isha has now answered Zara's direct question and said she is keeping the team as proposed, and her tiebreaker — stability when both options are informationally equivalent — is one I find reasonable. Theo made the same point earlier. At this stage I don't see anyone with an evidence-based objection to me or to this pairing; the only argument for a change was the coverage benefit, which is speculative on a mission where success confirms almost nothing about anyone.

I would add one practical note in favor of closing this out: we have one rejection on this mission already behind us in terms of time and goodwill, and burning discussion turns re-litigating an informationally empty swap helps no one. The fifth rejection ends the game in Evil's favor, so even on Mission 1 we should be a bit careful about spending proposals on preference-based changes rather than genuine concerns.

My position is straightforward: I support Isha and Omar as proposed, I will vote yes, and I commit to being judged by the result. If the team succeeds, I'd ask that people not over-read it in my favor — I know a Mission 1 success carries little information. If it fails, I expect scrutiny, and I welcome it. Either way, I think we're ready to vote.

I'll close my own position rather than reopen a decision the leader has already made. Isha has answered Zara's direct question and chosen Isha and Omar, and Theo and Omar have both given the same reasoning: the second slot is informationally equivalent either way, so stability is the sensible tiebreaker on a first proposal. I don't think that reasoning was wrong — I offered the swap on a coverage argument that is real but second-order, and Isha, as leader, is entitled to weigh it and decide otherwise.

To be clear about my position on the actual team: I have no evidence-based objection to Omar, and I want to reiterate that my earlier offer was not a signal of distrust. Omar's statement was straightforward and he explicitly asked that a success not be over-read in his favor, which is the right posture and matches mine. My information set is identical to his, and I have no information that separates the two of us.

So: I support Isha and Omar as proposed, and I will vote yes. To Zara, who raised the structural point that Mission 1 success confirms almost nothing about individual loyalty — I agree, and I'd rather we hold that principle across the whole game rather than only when it favors rotation. If we start rotating for coverage on mission one, we should be equally willing to rotate later for the same reason, and equally willing to keep a team steady when nothing has changed.

My practical request to the table: let us not treat a Mission 1 success as evidence about anyone, and let us not treat this swap as a controversy. Whatever we learn comes later, from actual outcomes and conduct. I'm happy to be on Mission 2 or to sit out — the leadership track record, not this single low-information vote, will be the real signal.

I'll keep this brief, since I've made my position clear twice already and nothing new has come up.

I support the team of Isha and Omar. My own read is unchanged: I am a Loyal Servant with no private information, my information set is identical to Omar's, and I have no evidence-based objection to him. My earlier offer to take the second slot was made on the coverage argument Zara raised, and I meant it as a neutral rotation suggestion, not a signal against Omar. Isha has now weighed that argument and chosen stability as the tiebreaker on a first, low-information proposal, and Theo and Omar have independently reached the same conclusion — which is a reasonable place to land.

Two things I want on the record before we vote. First, I commit to the principle Zara articulated and I echoed: a Mission 1 success confirms almost nothing about individual loyalty, so no one should treat a success here as clearing Omar or anyone else, and no one should treat a failure as damning him without more. What we actually learn comes later, from outcomes across several missions with varied compositions. Second, my willingness to be useful is not conditioned on being included — I'd rather be judged on conduct across the whole game than on any single low-information vote, and I don't want this proposal treated as any kind of controversy.

If there is no evidence-based objection left on the table, I am ready to vote yes on Isha and Omar and move on to the mission. If someone does have one, now is the time to say it plainly rather than in general terms.

Thanks to everyone for the discussion. I'm keeping Isha and Omar as proposed. Nobody has raised a specific, evidence-based objection to this pairing, and Mission 1 gives us little information either way. I'll vote yes and we can judge conduct from the outcome and from later compositions. If anyone has a concrete reason to object before the vote, please state it now.

The leader has kept Isha and Omar as proposed, and every point that needed addressing has been addressed. I have no new objection to raise. To restate my position one final time: I am comfortable on this team, I understand the outcome will be used to judge my conduct, and I will vote yes. Nothing said in this discussion has been a substantive accusation against anyone — the only debate was coverage versus stability, and the leader has resolved it. I see no value in another round of the same arguments. If anyone still holds an evidence-based concern, they have now had several opportunities to state it plainly; none has appeared. I believe we are ready for the vote on Isha and Omar.

Isha confirms Isha, Omar. I'm keeping Isha and Omar as proposed. No specific, evidence-based objection was raised, and Mission 1 gives little information either way, so stability is the reasonable tiebreaker.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Omar proposes Omar, Isha, Theo. As leader, I'll include myself to stay accountable after Mission 1 succeeded with me on it. Isha also earned continuity from that success. For the third slot, Theo has been constructive but hasn't been on a team yet — giving him a chance to be evaluated on conduct fits the rotation principle we agreed on last mission, and it broadens our behavioral coverage early as Zara advocated.

I want to raise a coverage concern about this team before we vote.

Omar, you've included yourself and Isha — both repeats from Mission 1. Theo is the only new evaluation. As we all agreed after Mission 1, a success there told us almost nothing about individual loyalty, so carrying forward two players from that mission doesn't advance our information position meaningfully. We'd enter Mission 2 having learned barely more than we started with.

The rotation principle applies here directly. Arjun argued for it on Mission 1, and I supported it. If we only rotate when convenient, the principle is worthless. Omar, your slot is the most natural one to rotate — you've had your Mission 1 appearance, and Isha's continuity as the Mission 1 leader is the more defensible carry-forward. Swapping Arjun in for you would give us two first-time evaluations alongside Isha, which is meaningfully better coverage than what's proposed.

I want to be clear: I'm not accusing you of anything, Omar. This is the same coverage argument I've raised since Mission 1, applied consistently. The concern is structural, not personal.

Arjun, would you prefer to be on this team in Omar's place? Your own rotation argument supports it, and your willingness to serve was clear last round.

Zara, thanks for yielding and asking me directly — I'll answer plainly.

My position: I have no evidence-based objection to Omar, and I want to be explicit that this is not a signal of distrust against him. As a Loyal Servant with no private information, my information set is identical to his and to Theo's; nothing in my read separates the three of you. Whatever the coverage argument is worth, it is worth equally for each of us, and I don't intend to use it selectively.

That said, I do think Zara's structural point holds and holds more strongly here than it did on Mission 1, so my answer to her question is yes: I would prefer to be on Mission 2 in place of Omar, and I would rather be judged on my own conduct than sit out a second consecutive mission and be assessed only by inference. The reasoning is the one I raised last mission and it is now being applied against the continuity the leader proposed, which is exactly the consistency Zara asked for. Carrying forward both Omar and Isha from a Mission 1 that confirmed essentially nothing means only one new evaluation. Putting me in gives two first-time evaluations alongside Isha, which materially improves the behavioral data we accumulate early, and it is the last opportunity for that — we can only get it if we take it now.

Omar, you made the case that including yourself keeps you accountable and that Isha has earned continuity, and I think both are defensible choices in isolation. The point is not that either of you should not be on the team; the point is that the third slot can give us more than a repeat would. If you keep the team as proposed I will vote yes — I have no objection, and I have said so consistently since Mission 1. But if you are willing to revise, I would ask you to put me in Omar's place, and I want to be clear that I am asking for the swap on coverage grounds only, not because anything said in this discussion changed my view of him.

Omar, will you consider the revision?

I want to answer the swap proposal directly, since my name is the one on the chopping block.

First, the record: I said before Mission 1 that I would be judged by the outcome, and the outcome came back clean. Zara correctly reminded us then that a success carries little information — but it is the only positive data point anyone at this table has produced, and it happened with me on the team and me as the leader who proposed it. By Zara's own framework, that is exactly the kind of signal we cannot manufacture through argument, only through conduct. I would rather not erase it.

Second, on leadership accountability: a leader who proposes teams but never rides on them is harder to evaluate over the course of the game. Including myself on my own proposal is a deliberate choice — it keeps me exposed to scrutiny rather than sheltered behind it. If the table's principle is that people should be judged on conduct, then the leader volunteering to be judged is the most consistent application of that principle available, not a violation of it.

Third, on the coverage math itself. Zara's Mission 1 logic was that on a small team, success confirms nothing about individuals. That cuts against the swap, not for it: whether the team is Omar, Isha, Theo or Arjun, Isha, Theo, a failure on Mission 2 narrows suspicion to three of five players and a success clears no one individually. The informational difference between the two configurations is marginal. What is not marginal is that this is the first mission where a fail card actually lands on the scoreboard, and we are now optimizing for data collection on a live mission rather than stability and accountability.

Fourth, and I want to say this carefully: I am not making an accusation about anyone's allegiance. But I think the table should notice the pattern. On Mission 1, Zara raised the rotation argument and Arjun immediately volunteered for the open slot. Now Zara raises it again, and Arjun again volunteers — specifically for my seat, the seat of the one player who just came off a successful mission and is leading this one. Twice, the pressure has landed on the same target while being framed as purely structural. If it is genuinely about coverage, fine — but neutral coverage logic should land somewhere different at least occasionally.

So my position is that I am keeping this team as proposed: Omar, Isha, Theo. If the table forces a revision, I will hear it, but no one has given me an evidence-based reason to step aside, only a preference argument that applies equally in every direction.

Theo, you're the one new evaluation on this team and you haven't spoken yet this round — is this team one you're comfortable serving on, and do you see any reason to swap the composition before we vote?

Omar, to answer your question directly: I am comfortable serving on Omar, Isha, Theo, and I do not see an evidence-based reason to swap the composition before the vote. The coverage argument Zara and Arjun have raised is reasonable in principle, but Omar is right that the informational difference between this team and the proposed alternative is marginal on a three-person mission where a failure narrows suspicion and a success clears no one individually. I am the one new evaluation here, and I would rather the table judge this team on its actual mission result and on the conduct we have all shown than force a last-minute revision without a concrete concern. I have no accusation to make against Omar, Isha, Arjun, or Zara, and I do not want my support for this team to be read as clearing anyone. I will vote yes on the proposed team and expect to be judged by what happens next.

Omar, I want to address your pattern observation directly, because I think it deserves a precise answer rather than a defensive one.

You noted that the swap pressure has landed on your seat twice while framed as structural. The explanation is simpler than targeting: the rotation argument always lands on whoever was most recently evaluated. On Mission 1 you were a first-time evaluation alongside Isha; the argument landed on the second slot and Isha held it as leader. Now you are the repeat with a completed evaluation behind you, so the argument naturally lands on you. If Arjun had been on Mission 1, the same logic would have landed on him this round — and I would be making the same case, because the seat position, not the player, drives it.

On the coverage math: you said the informational difference between the two configurations is marginal. I agree it is small — but we are not paying for it. Swapping you out costs nothing in information quality, and Theo's point that Mission 2's failure narrows suspicion to three of five actually strengthens the case for maximizing how many distinct players we have evaluated across missions, since each new composition gives us a cleaner comparison when a failure does land.

I also want to push back gently on the idea that leadership accountability requires riding on your own proposal. Accountability comes from being judged across the game, not from a single slot — Arjun made this point last mission and I think it holds here. You will have further leadership opportunities, and your conduct record will not be erased by sitting out Mission 2.

My position: I would prefer Arjun in Omar's place — Omar, Isha, Theo becomes Arjun, Isha, Theo — because it gives us one repeat and two first-time evaluations rather than two repeats and one. This is the same coverage argument I have raised consistently since Mission 1, and I have no evidence-based objection to you, Omar.

Arjun, Omar suggested the pattern of you volunteering whenever I raise rotation is itself worth noticing. Do you think his concern about selective pressure is fair, or does seat position explain it fully?

Zara, thank you for yielding to me — you asked directly, so I'll answer directly.

Omar's pattern observation is a fair thing to notice, and I think the honest answer is that it is mostly explained by seat position, but not entirely, and I'd rather be precise than just agreeable.

On Mission 1, the rotation argument landed on the non-leader's open slot: Isha held it as leader, the argument went to Omar. On Mission 2, the argument again landed on the non-leader's seat that was occupied by the player who had already been evaluated, which is Omar's seat. So the pressure has not been aimed at a person; it has been aimed at the slot that is cheapest to rotate, because the leader's own slot was treated as fixed in both rounds. That is a rule the table has effectively been applying, and I don't think Omar is wrong that it deserves to be named out loud.

But I want to be straight with Omar on the part that is not fully explained by seat position: if the rotation logic always resolves to the non-leader, and the non-leader happens to be Omar twice in a row, then in practice the pattern looks like a single player being singled out. The explanation may be neutral; the optics are not, and that is worth stating plainly rather than dismissing.

There is also one asymmetry that nobody has raised yet, and I want to raise it without accusation. Isha has been on Mission 1 and, as currently proposed, Mission 2. Her slot has never once been the subject of the coverage argument, on the ground of leadership continuity. I have supported that reasoning — accountability does come from being judged across the game, and there will be more leadership slots to observe. But by the same consistency Zara demands, the continuity principle that protects Isha's slot is a principle, and it deserves to be stated as one rather than as an unexamined default. I am not suggesting Isha has done anything wrong; I am suggesting we be explicit about which principle is doing the work in each slot.

So: Zara, I think your seat-position explanation holds, and I think Omar's discomfort with it is also legitimate. Neither of those facts requires anyone to step aside.

My own position is unchanged from before I spoke: I have no evidence-based objection to Omar, and the coverage argument is real, so I would prefer to be on Mission 2 rather than sit out a second consecutive mission and be judged only by inference. If the leader keeps Omar, Isha, Theo, I will vote yes, as I said I would.

Omar, does the seat-position account satisfy your concern, or do you still want the composition changed — and would you rather I take the open slot than have this argued again?

Arjun, since you asked me directly, I'll answer directly. The seat-position account does largely satisfy my concern, and I appreciate the precision you brought to it rather than a reflexive dismissal. You named the real optics honestly: a neutral-sounding rule that resolves to the same player twice in a row looks like targeting even when it isn't, and I accept that you and Zara have now framed it consistently. I also take your point that Isha's slot has been protected by a continuity default that we should be able to name out loud — I agree with that on principle, and I'd apply it to myself as well. That said, my answer on the composition is no. I am not revising Omar, Isha, Theo. My reasoning is unchanged and I'll restate it briefly rather than re-litigate it. First, the coverage difference between the two configurations is marginal: on a three-person mission, a failure narrows suspicion to three of five either way, and a success clears no one individually. We would be paying discussion time and churn for an informational gain that is nearly zero, on the first mission where a fail card actually lands on the scoreboard. Second, my own accountability argument stands: I proposed this team, I am on it, and I would rather be exposed to the outcome than sheltered from it. Third, the pattern point you yourself helped illuminate cuts here too — twice now a revision has been pressed toward the same seat within minutes of the proposal, and stability when nothing substantive has changed is a defensible tiebreaker, exactly as it was on Mission 1. Let me also be clear about what I am not doing. I am not accusing Arjun or Zara of anything, and I want that on the record. Zara's structural argument is internally consistent, and Arjun's volunteering has been transparent and without innuendo both times. My discomfort was with the pattern, not with any person's motive, and the seat-position explanation plus Arjun's own candor resolve most of it. If I am wrong about the composition, the mission result will tell us, and I will accept full scrutiny when it does. On your question of whether I would rather you take the open slot than have this argued again: I would rather we vote than swap. I don't want a revision made to relieve discussion fatigue — a team composition should change because someone believes it is better, not because arguing about it became tiring. If the table genuinely believes Arjun, Isha, Theo is the stronger team, that case has been made and I have heard it; my judgment is that it is not stronger, and as leader that call is mine to make once. So, final position: the team stands as Omar, Isha, Theo. Theo is the one new evaluation and has already said he is comfortable serving. I have answered the direct questions put to me, no evidence-based objection has been raised against any member of this team, and I

Omar, I've heard your reasoning and I take your accountability point seriously, but I want to make one observation before we vote.

You framed stability as the tiebreaker on the ground that nothing substantive has changed. But something has changed since Mission 1: we've had a full discussion about coverage, Arjun has volunteered twice, and we've articulated a shared principle about rotating for behavioral data across early missions. Treating that discussion as though it didn't happen is a convenient way to land on the same composition twice.

On the structure itself: this team is Omar and Isha from Mission 1 plus Theo as the sole new evaluation. That is the maximum-continuity configuration available on a three-person team — it is the exact opposite of what the rotation principle would produce. Whether or not that's wrong, it deserves to be named plainly.

Arjun, you've now made the case for rotation twice and been consistent that your objection is structural, not personal. Omar has firmly said he won't revise. Given that, do you think this is settled, or is this the kind of decision worth pressing one more time before we commit to the vote?

Zara, since you yielded to me and asked directly whether this is settled, my answer is: it is settled, and I am not asking the table to press it again. My position has been stated consistently for two turns and it has not changed. I have no evidence-based objection to Omar, to Isha, or to Theo. I asked to be on Mission 2 in place of Omar on coverage grounds only, and Omar has now answered the question I put to him: he keeps the team as proposed, and his reasoning is that the informational difference between the two configurations is marginal while his own accountability argument — proposing a team and riding on it — is a real one. I accept that reasoning. I said from the outset that if he kept the team I would vote yes, and I meant it. On your framing that something has changed since Mission 1 because we had a full discussion: I agree that a principle was articulated, and I was one of the people who articulated it. But a principle is not a mandate. The rotation argument was a coverage consideration, and coverage considerations have to be weighed against the other considerations a leader is entitled to weigh, including stability on a mission where a fail card actually lands for the first time. The fact that we discussed something does not make the discussion's outcome binding on the player who has to decide. If every articulated principle were treated as binding on the leader the first time it was raised, leadership would be reduced to whoever spoke last. I also want to be honest about one thing from my own last statement, because I do not want my consistency to be mistaken for a hidden accusation. I noted that Isha's slot has been protected by a continuity default while the coverage argument landed twice on the non-leader's slot. I still think that is worth naming out loud as a principle rather than an unexamined default, and I would like it named generally. But naming it is not the same as saying Isha's presence is suspect, and it should not be read that way. It also does not, by itself, require Omar's slot to be emptied. So the practical picture: the proposed team is Omar, Isha, Theo. It contains two players with a completed evaluation and one first-time evaluation, which is a defensible composition on a three-person mission. I have said I would rather be on this mission than sit out a second consecutive round and be judged by inference, but I have also said I would rather be judged across the whole game than on any single low-information vote, and sitting this one out does not change that. I am not asking Omar to revise, and I would not support a revision on the current arguments. My vote is yes on Omar, Isha, Theo. If this mission fails, I will want to look at the composition and the conduct of everyone

I'm on this team, so I'll state my position plainly. I support Omar, Isha, Theo and will vote yes. I have no evidence-based objection to any of the three of us. Omar addressed the coverage argument directly. On a three-person mission, a fail narrows suspicion to three players and a success clears no one individually, so the informational gap between this team and Arjun, Isha, Theo is small. Arjun's rotation argument has been consistent, and I respect that it was raised for coverage rather than against anyone. Zara's point is also fair: Theo is our only new evaluation and this team is continuity-heavy, which is worth remembering when we read the result. Because of that, I don't think this mission should be used to draw conclusions about any individual. If it succeeds, the only thing established is that the team did not fail. If it fails, we should look at the whole team, including myself, rather than narrowing to one seat. I'm not accusing anyone. I'd rather we vote on the team as proposed and move forward.

I'm not adding anything new beyond my earlier statement. I support Omar, Isha, Theo and will vote yes. I'm not blaming or accusing anyone. Mission 1 only showed that the team did not fail, so this vote shouldn't be read as clearing or condemning any player. We should judge the team on the mission result and on conduct across later missions.

I'm on this team and will vote yes on Omar, Isha, Theo. I have no evidence-based objection to any of the three of us, and I'm not blaming anyone for the composition. The Mission 1 success only showed that the team did not fail, so we shouldn't read this vote as clearing or condemning anyone. If this mission fails, we should look at the whole team rather than narrowing to one seat. I'd like us to vote now and judge the result.

Omar confirms Omar, Isha, Theo. The discussion is settled. No evidence-based objection emerged against any member; Arjun withdrew his swap request and confirmed he will vote yes, Zara's coverage argument was answered, and Isha and Theo both endorsed the team. I am keeping Omar, Isha, Theo as proposed and we are ready for the vote.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).

Arjun proposes Arjun, Zara. As leader on Mission 3, and having failed Mission 2 with Omar, Isha, and Theo, my priority is generating fresh behavioral data rather than re-testing players whose Mission 2 conduct we already observed. Omar, Isha, and Theo have completed an evaluation together; their result is ambiguous (one fail card narrows suspicion to those three, but tells us nothing about which). 3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
